extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics and mathematicians interested in 19th-century foundations and rigor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the normative standards, criteria, and evaluative distinctions used by early 19th-century analysts (Abel, Cauchy, contemporaries) when judging proofs, formulae, and operations on infinite series. Focuses on how exceptions, counterexamples, convergence, and modes of argument were treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule vs theorem distinction (exceptions allowed for rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 19th century a 'rule' could be perceived as a general statement for which 'exceptions' were possible; such rules were useful operationally even if not absolutely universal. By contrast, a modern 'theorem' is expected to be absolute and refutable by any counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Eulerian/formula-centered results were often regarded as rules that could survive presentation of a few exceptions. Volkert's phrase 'statistically using the ∀-quantifier' captures this: claims that seem to say 'for all' but in practice mean 'for almost all' or 'with some uninteresting exceptions.' When assessing historical work, note whether the author treats a statement as a rule (tolerant of exceptions) or as a precise theorem (intolerant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'exception' from 'counterexample'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'exception' (early 19th-century usage) is a special case that may invalidate a general application but not necessarily the value of the general rule; a 'counterexample' (modern sense) refutes a theorem and shows it false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Abel called certain singular examples 'exceptions' and sometimes accepted the general result as still valuable; later practice (and Abel in some contexts) treated similar instances as counterexamples that require reanalysis. When evaluating a claim, determine whether the author treats the instance as a tolerable exception or as a refutation requiring repair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require uniform convergence (or extra convergence hypotheses) for termwise operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations performed term-by-term (differentiation, integration, substitution, etc.) on infinite series require additional hypotheses—Cauchy amended Theorem C by adding a uniform convergence requirement to eliminate exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform convergence (or absolute convergence/other sufficient conditions) as the criterion that legitimizes passing operations through an infinite sum. The paper gives the historical example that adding an explicit uniform convergence requirement removes the kind of exception shown by Abel's/ Cauchy's series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't treat formal formulae as numerical truth without verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal equalities (general forms) cannot automatically be instantiated at particular parameter values; inserting specific values can lead to absurd numerical consequences unless the numerical correspondence is checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degen's warning: from sin φ + (1/2) sin 2φ + ... = (π−φ)/2 one must not naively set φ = 0 and infer 0+0+... = π/2. Always verify numerical convergence/validity before substituting values into formally derived equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of series of continuous functions does not imply continuity of the sum
rubrics_metrics.description: A series whose terms are continuous functions may converge to a discontinuous sum function at certain parameter values (example: the series shown by Abel is continuous in y when x<1 but at x=1 is convergent yet discontinuous for some y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the mode of convergence: uniform convergence of a series of continuous functions guarantees continuity of the sum; pointwise convergence does not. Use counterexamples (Abel's series, translations) to test claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termwise differentiation requires proof (may produce divergent series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiating an infinite series term-by-term is not automatically legitimate; doing so can produce a divergent series and thus a false equality (Abel exhibited such an example where differentiation gives a divergent cosine-series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying termwise differentiation, provide justification (uniform convergence of the differentiated series, or other sufficient hypotheses). The absence of such a proof is an anti-pattern in rigorous analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state restrictions and domain of validity for general algebraic deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many formula-centered manipulations hold 'in general' but fail in particular special cases; authors should state 'certain restrictions' or caveats when asserting general formulae (Abel often used phrasing like 'in general, except in certain particular cases').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting results derived from formal manipulations (e.g., degree-operator arguments), explicitly enumerate or at least acknowledge exceptional cases rather than leaving them implicit. This improves rigor and clarifies applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single universal multiplicative test function for convergence exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Abel refuted Olivier's proposed criterion (that ∑ a_n converges iff n a_n → 0) and proved more generally that no function φ(n) can serve so that ∑ a_n convergent ⇔ φ(n)a_n → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek or claim a single φ(n) that uniformly decides series convergence by multiplication; employ a variety of appropriate classical tests instead and be cautious of purported universal testers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count/quantity of exceptions matters for assessing severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors assessed the seriousness of a defect by the number of exceptions: 'indefinitely many' exceptions indicate a more severe problem than an isolated special case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a claimed general rule, record whether exceptions are isolated/finite or infinite/dense; many exceptions suggest that the rule's domain is fundamentally misstated and caution is warranted in applying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between formula-centered and concept-centered modes of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Formula-centered mathematics emphasizes formal manipulations and operational rules (tolerating exceptions and relying on practitioner intuition); concept-centered mathematics emphasizes precisely stated theorems, rigorous domain specifications, and proof analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mathematical work by which mode it follows. Formula-centered work may be acceptable in contexts valuing computational or representational utility but should still flag restrictions; concept-centered work must provide domain conditions and full justifications. Abel used both modes in different parts of his oeuvre (elliptic-function work vs convergence/rigor work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to analyze and repair (or delimit) theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: In the concept-centered tradition, a counterexample is used to demonstrate falsity of a theorem and to prompt an analysis that refines or repairs the theorem by precisely determining its valid domain and necessary hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterexample is produced, follow with analysis that identifies why the theorem failed and propose amended hypotheses (for example, adding uniform convergence). Abel applied this approach in his critique of Olivier's convergence criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify algebraic equalities involving degree/leading-term arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations such as deg(P1+P2) = max{deg P1, deg P2} need verification when deg P1 = deg P2; such equalities hold 'in general' but may fail in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using degree-based or leading-term heuristics in algebraic arguments, either prove the equality in the relevant case or explicitly note the exceptional parameter configurations where it fails.
